question:
A homogeneous, isotropic single-layer x–y model has geometry, recharge, and west/east CHD heads that
are uniform in y. Its north/south boundaries are no-flow. Which predictions are justified? (Select
ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. With geometry and forcing independent of y, a y-independent solution has no north/south
flow and can satisfy the two-dimensional equations. Recharge and the west/east heads can still
produce head variation in x. Adding a coordinate direction does not by itself invalidate an
analytical solution for the corresponding symmetric problem.
error:
Not quite. A no-flow condition on the north/south sides constrains flow across those sides; it does
not require head to be constant in x. Check whether anything in the physical inputs breaks the
symmetry in y before predicting a north/south head gradient.

question:
How does computational size change when square horizontal grids and additional layers are used?
(Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. Horizontal cell count grows as N² for an N × N grid, and adding layers multiplies that
count again. Larger systems can require more work per iteration without requiring more iterations.
Total cells and unknown active heads are not identical counts because prescribed-head or inactive
cells are treated separately.
error:
Not quite. Multiply the counts in all spatial directions. Then distinguish the number of equations
and the work in each iteration from the number of iterations needed to meet the stopping criteria.

question:
You compare MODFLOW-2005 PCG, MODFLOW-NWT GMRES, and MODFLOW 6 CG on the same two-dimensional case.
Which statements support a fair interpretation? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. A controlled comparison preserves the intended hydraulic problem and starting conditions
while recording each engine's numerical formulation and settings. Equal threshold numbers are not
sufficient when residual definitions, norms, or iteration levels differ. The tested combinations
differ in more than their inner linear-solver names.
error:
Not quite. Check what each reported criterion and iteration count means. Also distinguish a change
of inner linear solver from a change of engine and nonlinear formulation. Comparing different
hydraulic inputs would introduce an additional source of differences.

question:
Conductivity is now allowed to vary randomly in both x and y, while the west/east CHD heads remain
uniform in y. Which statements are correct? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. Spatial variations in conductivity can redirect flow and break the y symmetry even when the
boundary heads remain uniform along those boundaries. The spatial arrangement matters as well as the
mean. Reusing the actual conductivity array isolates engine differences for a fixed realization.
error:
Not quite. Boundary symmetry does not remove conductivity variation inside the domain. Compare the
complete spatial field, and distinguish an engine comparison from an experiment that changes the
hydraulic conductivity realization.

question:
The aquifer bottom is 0 m and the west/east CHD heads remain positive. What can be inferred when
changing the initial guesses in the variable-head cells? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. Initial guesses influence the numerical path while the CHD heads remain prescribed. In a
convertible aquifer, near-bottom guesses can imply very small saturated thickness in variable-head
cells. Random guesses can be more or less favourable than a uniform guess; their effect must be
measured rather than assumed.
error:
Not quite. Distinguish the prescribed boundary heads from the numerical estimates in the interior.
Relate each estimate to saturated thickness, and avoid assuming that a random initial field is
always farther from the eventual solution.

question:
Before extending the model from a single layer to three dimensions, which checks are appropriate?
(Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. A three-dimensional extension changes the system size and can resolve vertical gradients or
different saturation states with depth. Those changes require inspection beyond a horizontal head
profile. Homogeneity alone does not establish the assumptions of a reduced one-dimensional solution,
and a successful simpler calculation does not guarantee that the larger problem will converge.
error:
Not quite. Check both computational size and the additional hydraulic behaviour that vertical
discretization permits. Treat the analytical reference and convergence of the simpler model as
useful evidence, not as guarantees for the layered calculation.
